clinicalPearls: SPG1 is an X-linked complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by pathogenic variants in L1CAM at Xq28; it affects males, with female carriers usually spared or only mildly affected.

It sits within the L1 syndrome (CRASH) spectrum, so the same gene can produce X-linked hydrocephalus with aqueductal stenosis, agenesis of the corpus callosum, MASA syndrome and spastic paraplegia, sometimes within one family.
The MASA acronym (intellectual disability, aphasia or delayed speech, shuffling spastic gait, adducted thumbs) captures the characteristic complicated phenotype.
Bilaterally adducted or clasped thumbs are a valuable bedside clue and may also be detectable in obligate female carriers.
Cognitive impairment and expressive language delay commonly accompany the lower-limb spasticity, distinguishing it from pure autosomal HSP.
Brain imaging may show ventriculomegaly, aqueductal stenosis, a hypoplastic or absent corpus callosum and small or absent pyramids.
Marked intrafamilial and interfamilial variability means severity cannot be reliably predicted from the specific variant.
Antenatal ventriculomegaly in a male fetus with a relevant family history should prompt consideration of L1CAM analysis.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG1 arises from loss-of-function variants in L1CAM on chromosome Xq28, which encodes the L1 cell adhesion molecule, a transmembrane neuronal glycoprotein of the immunoglobulin superfamily. L1 mediates homophilic and heterophilic cell-cell adhesion and drives neurite outgrowth, axon guidance and fasciculation, neuronal migration, myelination and synaptic remodelling during nervous system development. Disruption of these functions impairs formation and guidance of long descending tracts, particularly the corticospinal pathways and the pyramidal decussation, and interferes with development of the corpus callosum and patency of the cerebral aqueduct. The resulting maldevelopment explains the spectrum that ranges from severe congenital hydrocephalus with aqueductal stenosis at one extreme to a comparatively milder complicated spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability and adducted thumbs at the other, all reflecting the degree of residual L1 function.
additionalDifferentials: SPG2 (PLP1-related), the other classic X-linked complicated HSP and allelic with Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease

Autosomal recessive complicated HSP with thin corpus callosum (SPG11, SPG15)
Cerebral palsy of spastic diplegic type, especially where perinatal history is misleading
Other X-linked intellectual disability syndromes featuring spasticity
Corpus callosum agenesis syndromes of differing genetic cause
additionalInvestigations: Molecular analysis of L1CAM by sequencing with copy-number/deletion testing
MRI of the brain assessing the aqueduct, ventricles, corpus callosum and pyramids
Detailed X-linked pedigree construction and maternal carrier testing
Antenatal ultrasound surveillance for ventriculomegaly in at-risk pregnancies
Developmental and cognitive assessment with speech and language evaluation
Examination for adducted thumbs and other subtle skeletal signs in relatives
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging head circumference or clinical signs of raised intracranial pressure from progressive hydrocephalus
Severe neonatal hydrocephalus requiring urgent neurosurgical assessment for shunting
New bulbar or brainstem signs suggesting evolving structural compromise
Acute deterioration in a child with a known shunt (possible obstruction or infection)
reference.prognosis: Outcome is highly variable and correlates broadly with the severity of the underlying malformation, ranging from perinatal death or profound disability in severe congenital hydrocephalus to survival with variable spasticity, intellectual disability and language impairment at the milder MASA end. Progression of the spastic paraplegia itself is generally slow once early development is complete.
pitfalls: Labelling the presentation as isolated congenital hydrocephalus or cerebral palsy and overlooking the underlying L1CAM disorder and its inheritance implications
Assuming female carriers are entirely unaffected, when subtle signs such as adducted thumbs may be present
Predicting severity from the variant alone, given the wide phenotypic range within families
Failing to offer genetic counselling and carrier testing across the maternal line
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
GeneReviews: Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia Overview and L1 Syndrome
management: Manage hydrocephalus and aqueductal stenosis neurosurgically with ventricular shunting where present
Control spasticity with antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine, physiotherapy and orthoses, using botulinum toxin for focal problems such as adducted thumbs
Provide developmental support with speech and language therapy for expressive delay and educational support for intellectual disability
Offer orthopaedic management of adducted or clasped thumbs and other skeletal deformities
Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric neurology, neurosurgery, rehabilitation and developmental services
Offer genetic counselling for X-linked L1CAM inheritance with maternal carrier testing and antenatal ultrasound surveillance for ventriculomegaly in at-risk pregnancies
